brief.title: The cost of annual milestones in school connectivity planning: evidence from Honduras
brief.subtitle: Policy brief on a multi-period mixed-integer programme for 12,578 unconnected public schools, over a five-year horizon, with a US$125M budget
meta: Multi-period MILP; Julia/JuMP with Gurobi, 5% MIP gap

blocks.text: Honduras's public school system is largely offline. Of 15,492 public schools in the Giga dataset, 1,130 (7.3%) have an internet connection [@giga; @report]. This brief evaluates how a fixed budget of US$125M over five years should be spent to connect the remaining schools with fixed wireless (WISP) infrastructure, and what it costs to require visible progress in each year.

A multi-period mixed-integer linear programme (MILP) connects 12,409 of the 12,578 schools in scope (98.7%) by year 5 when the timing of investment is unrestricted. Requiring cumulative annual milestones of 10% to 30% of schools reduces this to 9,363 (74.4%) on an identical budget: a loss of 3,046 schools, or 24.2 percentage points.

The loss arises from operating cost rather than a shortage of capital. Each connected school incurs US$3,820 a year in operations and maintenance (O&M), charged against the same budget as construction, so schools connected early consume funds that would otherwise build infrastructure. For each additional school connected before year 5, approximately 1.06 schools are forgone at year 5.

The loss is also geographically concentrated. Under milestones, Islas de la Bahía, Olancho, Yoro and Francisco Morazán finish below 37% coverage against 74.4% nationally. These departments depend most on new towers at US$100,000 each, while budget is allocated in proportion to unconnected schools rather than to the cost of connecting them.

Confidence reflects how directly each judgement follows from the model output. High: read directly from the model output. Moderate: the figures are reproduced, but the explanation or the dependency on a cost assumption is interpretive.

items.text: Annual milestones reduce year-5 coverage by 3,046 schools (24.2 percentage points) at an identical budget.

The reduction is driven by O&M. The milestone plan accrues US$23.3M in O&M within the horizon against US$0.3M for the unrestricted plan. Its capital spend is US$34.0M lower, of which US$23.0M is absorbed by O&M and US$10.9M is left unspent.
Without targets, the model defers activation to the final year: 99.4% of connections and 94% of WISP installations fall in year 5, while towers, which carry no O&M, are built throughout.
Milestones strand equipment. 1,183 device packages (US$8.6M) are delivered to schools that are not connected by year 5, against 40 (US$0.3M) in the unrestricted plan.
Departmental shortfalls under milestones are driven by dependence on new towers combined with allocation by school count rather than by cost.
items.basis: Model output; mechanism not tested by an alternative allocation run

items.text: Both plans create a recurring O&M commitment that the capital budget does not fund: US$47.4M a year from 2030 under the unrestricted plan and US$35.8M under milestones.
items.basis: Exact arithmetic; depends on the US$3,820 point estimate

blocks.text: 1.1 Education and connectivity in Honduras

School connectivity bears directly on two targets of Sustainable Development Goal 4: target 4.1, universal completion of free and equitable primary and secondary education, and target 4.a, upgrading education facilities to provide effective learning environments [@sdg4]. ITU and UNDP report that digital technologies directly support 70% of SDG targets [@itu_undp]. In Honduras the need is acute. The World Bank estimates learning poverty, the share of children unable to read and understand a simple text by age 10, at 74.7% [@wb2021], and classrooms in developing countries are frequently overcrowded, with scarce teaching materials [@masino].

Giga, a joint initiative of UNICEF and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) launched in 2019, aims to connect every school in the world to the internet. It maintains an open, regularly updated map of school locations and connectivity status, built from government records and open sources [@giga; @gigamaps]. Its Honduras dataset records 15,492 public schools, of which 1,130 (7.3%) are connected. An earlier assessment cited by UNICEF Honduras put school connectivity at 6%, concentrated in urban areas, and found that 44% of schools lacked electricity [@unicefhn].

Connectivity is sharply divided by geography. Rural schools make up 86% of the total, and 3.6% of them are connected, against 29.9% of urban schools. Departmental rates range from 28.4% in Islas de la Bahía to 0.6% in Gracias a Dios [@report].
1.2 The planning problem

The government's allocation problem has three features that make simple, year-by-year planning inadequate. First, connecting a school requires several dependent investments: a tower, wireless equipment mounted on it, and equipment at the school. A tower built early yields no connection until the later investments complete it. Second, the cost of reaching a school differs by an order of magnitude depending on whether a tower already stands within range. Third, every connection carries a recurring cost that competes with new construction for the same funds. The question is therefore not only which schools to connect, but in what order and with which infrastructure.
1.3 Related work

The formulation extends the maximal covering location problem (MCLP) of Church and ReVelle, which selects a fixed number of facilities to maximise the demand covered within a service distance [@church]. Here schools are demand points, tower sites are facilities and the service distance is the WISP radius. Installing WISP on an existing tower (US$5,500) and building a new tower (US$100,000) differ in cost by a factor of 18, so the facility-count constraint is replaced by a budget constraint. Daskin notes that budget is the underlying reason for limiting the number of facilities in covering models [@daskin]. Reviews of facility location identify the integration of multiple layers and multiple periods as a persistent gap in single-period, single-layer covering models [@melo].

Multi-period, multi-layer formulations are better developed in rural electrification. Ferrer-Martí et al. jointly optimise generator location, sizing and microgrid layout, but in a single period [@ferrer]. Juanpera et al. plan electrification in stages at regional scale [@juanpera], and Yazıcı et al. optimise technology choice and network design over a multistage horizon [@yazici]. Correia and Melo model facilities whose investment satisfies demand only in later periods, the same temporal coupling as the tower–WISP–device chain [@correia]. The formulation summarised in Section 3 combines budgeted covering, a three-layer prerequisite chain, multi-period phasing and soft annual milestones, which none of these studies does in combination [@report].

The model draws on three sources. School locations, connectivity status and the condition of existing devices come from Giga [@giga]. Tower locations come from OpenCellID, an open crowd-sourced database of cellular base stations [@opencellid]. Its 9,230 records for Honduras reduce to 7,297 unique sites once co-located radio technologies are merged. Where no existing tower covers a school, candidate new-tower positions are generated at unserved school locations [@report]. Department boundaries on the map are from geoBoundaries [@geob].

blocks.text: For a school served alone, these figures imply about US$12,800 where an existing tower is in range and about US$112,800 where a tower must be built: a ratio of roughly 9:1. Where several schools share one WISP-equipped tower, the cost per school is lower.
3.1 The prerequisite chain

A school is defined as connected in a given year when two conditions hold simultaneously: it holds a device package, and at least one tower within 10 km carries operational WISP equipment. WISP equipment can be mounted only on a standing tower. Investment therefore follows a fixed order.

steps.label: WISP unit
steps.detail: US$5,500; requires a standing tower; serves schools within 10 km

steps.label: Connected
steps.detail: O&M of US$3,820 a year from the following year

blocks.text: Two properties of the chain shape the solution. Upstream investment produces nothing until every downstream layer is in place, so a tower built in year 1 yields no connection until WISP and devices follow. WISP coverage is also shared: one unit can serve every school within range, so the cost per school falls where schools cluster around a site. All three layers must therefore be planned jointly across the horizon.

blocks.text: 3.3 Objectives

Both models share every constraint and differ only in whether milestones are active. The unrestricted model maximises schools connected in year 5, with \(\lambda_t = 0\) so that no shortfall arises. It gives the solver full freedom over timing and sets an upper bound on coverage for the budget.

The milestone-constrained model maximises the same quantity less a penalty for falling short of the annual targets. The penalty \(\pi = 10\) is set so that the solver pursues the targets but abandons them where the O&M burden of meeting them outweighs the penalty [@report].
3.4 Constraints

blocks.label: Single installation
blocks.tex: \sum_{t \in T} x^{\mathrm{tow}}_{k,t} \le 1 - a^{\mathrm{tow}}_k, \quad \sum_{t \in T} x^{\mathrm{wisp}}_{k,t} \le 1 \;\; \forall k; \qquad \sum_{t \in T} x^{\mathrm{dev}}_{s,t} \le 1 - a^{\mathrm{dev}}_s \;\; \forall s
blocks.says: Each asset is installed at most once, and never where it already exists.

blocks.label: Precedence
blocks.tex: \sum_{\tau \le t} x^{\mathrm{wisp}}_{k,\tau} \;\le\; a^{\mathrm{tow}}_k + \sum_{\tau \le t} x^{\mathrm{tow}}_{k,\tau} \qquad \forall k,\, t
blocks.says: WISP can be installed at a site only if a tower stands there by that year.

blocks.label: Coverage
blocks.says: A school is covered only if at least one site in range carries WISP.

blocks.label: Connectivity
blocks.tex: Z_{s,t} \le \mathrm{cov}_{s,t}, \qquad Z_{s,t} \;\le\; a^{\mathrm{dev}}_s + \sum_{\tau \le t} x^{\mathrm{dev}}_{s,\tau} \qquad \forall s,\, t
blocks.says: A school is connected only if it is covered and holds devices. Together, (4) to (6) encode the prerequisite chain.

blocks.label: Persistence
blocks.says: A connection, once made, is maintained.

blocks.label: Capital spending
blocks.tex: \mathrm{capex}_t = \sum_{k} \big( c^{\mathrm{tow}} x^{\mathrm{tow}}_{k,t} + c^{\mathrm{wisp}} x^{\mathrm{wisp}}_{k,t} \big) + \sum_{s} c^{\mathrm{dev}} x^{\mathrm{dev}}_{s,t} \qquad \forall t

blocks.label: O&M spending
blocks.says: O&M is charged from the year after connection. A school connected in year 1 therefore incurs 4 × 3,820 = US$15,280 by year 5.

blocks.label: Cumulative budget
blocks.says: Spending to date may not exceed the budget released to date, so unspent funds roll over. Because O&M enters the same constraint as capital, early connections reduce later construction.

blocks.label: Milestones
blocks.says: Connected schools plus shortfall meet the cumulative target each year. Inactive when \(\lambda_t = 0\).

blocks.text: 3.5 Solution approach

The national problem, 12,578 schools by 7,297 existing sites over five years, is too large to solve directly, so it is decomposed by department. Departments are solved in sequence from the largest to the smallest number of unconnected schools, with \(S\) and \(K\) restricted to \(S_e\) and \(K_e\). Each department receives an annual budget of US$25M multiplied by its share of unconnected schools, and funds it leaves unspent are carried forward to the next department in the queue. The models are implemented in Julia/JuMP and solved with Gurobi to a relative MIP gap of 5% [@report].

items.text: All schools are assumed to have electricity, which is the responsibility of the national utility, ENEE. Around 44% of schools lack it [@unicefhn], so the results are an upper bound unless electrification proceeds in parallel.
Towers are WISP-compatible; infrastructure is installed in the year funded and operates thereafter; towers and WISP units have no capacity limit.
Coverage is a fixed 10 km Haversine radius, restricted to the three nearest towers per school for tractability. Line of sight, terrain, spectrum and backhaul are not modelled.
WISP only. Fibre and satellite are excluded, which is why 1,784 schools with no candidate tower in range fall outside the model.
Point estimates, independent of scale, with no inflation, discounting or procurement variance.
Deterministic at US$25M a year, allocated by unconnected-school count. Sequential decomposition by department means funds are not reallocated nationally, so the result is not a national optimum.
Each subproblem is solved to a 5% MIP gap. Reported plans are within 5% of the best plan for each department under these assumptions, not proven optima.
Service quality, institutional capacity, regulation, device maintenance cycles, and risks such as delays or vandalism [@report].

blocks.text: 5.1 Headline comparison
Table 3 compares the two plans. Both operate under the same budget, horizon, costs and coverage rules; the only difference is whether milestones are active.
5.2 Why the unrestricted plan defers activation

Without targets, the solver builds towers throughout the horizon (79, 53, 107, 56 and 35 a year) but installs 94% of WISP units and makes 99.4% of connections in year 5. Towers incur no O&M, whereas a connected school does. Activating every connection in the final year avoids up to four years of O&M per school, US$15,280, and releases those funds for further construction. Six departments (Lempira, Santa Bárbara, Cortés, Copán, Intibucá and Atlántida) reach full coverage of their in-scope schools. Of the 169 schools not reached, 96 are in Olancho.
5.3 The cost of milestones

Milestones force connections forward. The milestone plan makes 2,943 connections in years 1 to 4 (31% of its total), against 72 in the unrestricted plan, and accrues US$23.3M of O&M over the horizon against US$0.3M. Its capital programme is smaller by 1,607 device packages, 166 new towers and 1,023 WISP units. The capital gap of US$34.0M decomposes into US$23.0M of additional O&M and US$10.9M of budget left unspent, as departments that cannot meet early targets cheaply hold funds they cannot deploy productively. Each of the 2,871 additional early connections costs about 1.06 connections at year 5. The milestone plan also delivers 1,183 device packages (US$8.6M) to schools that never receive coverage within the horizon.
5.4 Departmental exposure

Budget is allocated in proportion to unconnected schools, not to the cost of reaching them. In the unrestricted plan, deferral keeps O&M close to zero, and most departments can fund the towers they need from their allocation. Under milestones, each department must show progress every year from the same allocation, and those that depend on new towers fall behind. Islas de la Bahía (24.4%), Olancho (29.8%), Yoro (31.6%) and Francisco Morazán (36.4%) finish furthest below the national figure of 74.4%, followed by Gracias a Dios (44.2%). These are among the most remote departments, where connecting a school often requires a new tower rather than WISP on an existing one [@report].

items.head: Calibrate milestones to the O&M–capital trade-off
items.text: The 24.2-point gap is driven by cumulative O&M. Relaxing targets in years 1 and 2 and concentrating them in years 3 to 5 would allow infrastructure to be built before connections are activated, preserving visible progress at lower cost [@report]. This schedule has not yet been modelled and is the most direct next run.

items.head: Allocate budget by cost to connect, or set a regional floor
items.text: Allocation in proportion to school count systematically underfunds departments that require new towers. A cost-weighted allocation, or a minimum coverage level per department, would target Islas de la Bahía, Olancho, Yoro and Francisco Morazán at some cost to national coverage, while narrowing the regional gap [@report].

items.head: Fund O&M before activating connections
items.text: Full coverage implies US$47.4M a year in O&M from 2030, equivalent to 38% of the five-year capital budget, every year. A standing O&M budget line is a precondition for the programme to sustain its own results [@report].

items.head: Treat out-of-range schools as a separate programme
items.text: The 1,784 excluded schools, and the 111 unreached schools with no site within 10 km, cannot be served by WISP at any budget. They require fibre or satellite, a different cost structure and possibly a different delivery body [@report].

blocks.text: Further work

items: Solve the national problem jointly, or with budget transfers between departments, to measure the cost of sequential decomposition.
Add per-site capacity and line-of-sight constraints, which the current coverage rule omits.
Couple the model to electrification planning, so that the 44% of schools without power enter as a joint constraint rather than an assumption.

Computers and school-side wireless equipment for one school.
Mixed-integer linear programme: an optimisation model with linear objective and constraints in which some decisions are restricted to whole numbers, here yes-or-no.
The relative difference between the best plan found and the solver's bound on the best possible plan.

mismatches.head: Duplicate site records in the milestone output
mismatches.text: MilestonesSites.csv holds 6,261 rows for 5,307 distinct sites; 921 sites appear more than once, and 68 of these carry contradictory WISP flags. The report's totals of 164 new towers and 313 WISP units count rows. Counting distinct sites gives 156 and 302, which would lower milestone CAPEX from US$84.5M to US$83.7M. The unrestricted output contains no duplicates.
mismatches.resolution: Headline figures keep the report's row counts for consistency with the report. The map draws each site once.

mismatches.head: The schools-per-percentage-point figure is a unit conversion
mismatches.text: The old README gave about 250 schools per percentage point, which was arithmetically wrong. The corrected figure, 3,046 / 24.22 ≈ 125.8, is simply 1% of 12,578 schools and carries no information about the trade-off.
mismatches.resolution: Replaced with a behavioural ratio: 1.06 schools forgone at year 5 for each additional school connected in years 1–4 (3,046 / 2,871).

mismatches.head: Not all 169 unreached schools lie outside coverage
mismatches.text: The report states that the 169 schools the unrestricted plan does not connect lie beyond any candidate tower's 10 km radius. Against the output files, 111 have no site within 10 km and 24 have a WISP-equipped site in range but no device package. The remaining 34 hold devices and have a WISP-equipped site in range, at a median distance of 5.6 km, yet are not connected. The stated connection rule does not explain these cases; a per-site capacity limit or a narrower school–site adjacency in the solver is the likely cause.
mismatches.resolution: The claim is not repeated. The school–site links drawn on the map are derived from distance, not exported from the solver.

mismatches.head: Setup figures cannot be recomputed from the published files
mismatches.text: The published files contain the 7,297 existing tower sites but not the candidate new-tower locations, and the baseline school list contains duplicate records. The figures of 15,492 schools, 1,130 connected and 1,784 excluded therefore cannot be reproduced and are taken from the report.
mismatches.resolution: Carried from the report with source notes. No baseline school layer is drawn.
